questions.q: What is the main architectural drawback of RBAC as fine-grained distinctions multiply?
options: RBAC cannot be audited at all
Roles multiply quickly, since every new fine distinction needs its own role
RBAC only works with unstructured data
RBAC requires attribute evaluation at request time
questions.explain: The lesson gives the example of "analysts who can see EU but not US customers" becoming its own role — RBAC scales roles, not rules.

questions.q: What does ABAC evaluate to make an access decision?
options: A fixed list of roles defined once at setup
Attributes of the user, the data, and the request context, at the moment access is requested
The physical location of the database server only
Only the user's job title, with no other context
questions.explain: ABAC decisions are evaluated dynamically against attributes of the user, data, and context — not a static role assignment.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say query-time (engine-level) enforcement is architecturally stronger than application-time enforcement?
options: Query-time enforcement is always faster to configure
It applies no matter which tool issues the query, while application-time filtering can be bypassed by anyone with direct engine access
Application-time enforcement is illegal under most data regulations
Query-time enforcement eliminates the need for any access control at all
questions.explain: Application-level filtering only protects users of that one application; direct access to the engine bypasses it entirely.

questions.q: Row-level security and column-level security differ in what way?
options: Row-level security restricts which rows are returned; column-level security restricts or masks specific columns, independent of rows
Row-level security only applies to numeric columns
Column-level security can only be applied to an entire table at once, never one column
They are two names for the exact same mechanism
questions.explain: The two operate on different axes of the same table and can be combined for a single query.

questions.q: According to the lesson, why is writing an access-control policy against a tag (rather than a hardcoded column list) architecturally significant?
options: Tag-based policies are the only way to achieve row-level security
Tags eliminate the need for authentication entirely
Tags make the underlying data encrypted automatically
A new column tagged the same way automatically inherits the same enforcement, with no policy rewrite required
questions.explain: This is the active-metadata bridge from the catalog (Chapter 3) to enforcement (Chapter 4): the tag, not a static column list, drives the policy.
